    segue

    segue is a package designed to help people transition from SAS to R with a focus on clinical statistics. Some issues that make that transition difficult are:

    • SAS has a more limited number of options than R. It is often hard to discover if there is an R package that fits their needs, and when there are many options, picking the one that is optimal.
    • SAS has a very unified syntax; R does not. Overall, there is a huge strength for R, but for someone new, it can be a nightmare.
    • There are methodological differences between the languages, even for commonly used methods. Also, defaults between the two can be different and produce different results.
    • SAS has copious amounts of generally good documentation. R often has fantastic documentation, but more often than not, it is lacking or poorly written for users.
    • R revels in lazy computations; it often gives you a minimal amount of returned values and printed output, and you can ask for more. SAS tends to dump everything on you, even if you didn’t really need it.

    Most of these issues are not technical problems. segue is meant to be a way for SAS folks to use R in a way that meets them in the middle. It repackages existing R functions such that:

    • They are discoverable. Naming is hard but important, and segue has a taxonomy built into its names that should make things obvious.
    • The computations for each function are well documented so that the user can understand what they will get. We can explicitly show the underlying R code and its SAS analog.
    • Compatibility is also documented. If there are numerical differences between SAS and R implementations of the same thing, how large are they?
    • Defaults are biased towards those from SAS. In almost any case, there is no uniformly “right” choice, but we can make the transition easier with judicious choices.
    • Errors are more informative than what base R would produce.
    • In some cases, the R API isn’t great (e.g., binom.test()) and the segue functions have a different interface.

    Installation

    You can install segue from CRAN with:

    install.packages("segue")

    You can install the development version of segue like so:

    install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("posit-dev/segue")

    Example

    bin_prop_test() tests a single binomial proportion using a two-level factor. Here, we test whether the proportion of patients with cognitive impairment is 0.5:

    library(segue)

cog_ability <- modeldata::ad_data$Class
table(cog_ability)
#> cog_ability
#> Impaired  Control 
#>       91      242

test_res <- bin_prop_test(cog_ability)
test_res
#> Testing a Single Binomial Proportion via exact Test
#> No missing values

    The results can be tidied into a tibble:

    tidy(test_res)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>   estimate statistic  p.value parameter conf.low conf.high method    alternative
#>      <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>     <chr>      
#> 1    0.273        91 5.86e-17       333    0.226     0.325 Exact bi… two.sided

    translate() shows the R code that was used, along with the analogous SAS code:

    translate(test_res)
#> ── R Code template ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> stats::binom.test(x = 91L, n = 333L, alternative = "two.sided", 
#>     p = 0.5)
#> 
#> ── SAS Code template ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> No known SAS equivalent
